newsitem.title: UK: MPs tell UK lottery regulator to get tough.
newsitem.headline: MPs tell UK lottery regulator to get tough.

text.p: Parliament's Public Accounts Committee told lottery regulator Peter Davis on Wednesday to get tougher with Camelot, the consortium running Britain's lottery.

Robert Sheldon, chairman of the powerful all-party committee, told Davis that regulators of other industries investigated by the panel had been "more vigorous" in their work. "We'd like you to bear that in mind," Sheldon said.
Camelot is a consortium owned by Cadbury Schweppes Plc, GTECH Holdings Corp, De La Rue Plc and Racal Electronics Plc, which each have 22.5 percent, and Japan's Fujitsu, which owns 10 percent.

Sheldon had been quizzing Davis about why he had not got Camelot to agree to pay interest on the prize payment shortfall -- the extent to which it falls short of its target, laid down in its licence, to pay a specified level of prizes.
The shortfall, which is held as part of Camelot's general balances, reached 135 million pounds in the year ended March 1996, earning Camelot six million pounds interest.

Davis said it was not within his powers to claw back the interest. He had approached the consortium but it had refused to renegotiate the existing arrangement unless it could renegotiate other aspects of its licence.
The committee was grilling Davis about a report in August by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), parliament's spending watchdog.
One member of the panel, Labour's Alan Williams, said the NAO study was a catalogue of administrative incompetence and "as damning as any report I've ever seen".
He said all the failings detected by the NAO had benefited Camelot and none had benefited the public or good causes.

Williams accused Davis of being "dilatory" and "unimaginative" in not pressing Camelot to divulge more information to the CAG, who said in his report he had been denied access to the consortium's accounts.
"Half the trouble is your lack of curiosity," Williams said. "There seems to be very little you do regard as important."

Davis, who said he did not have the legal power to require Camelot to open its books to the CAG, defended his record and said the NAO report found that all lottery proceeds for good causes were paid punctually and in full.
